6.198.m: The Kumāras said: / “Now we shall explain to you the injunctions for the seven-day listening session, / by which the Bhāgavata succeeds for men whose souls are offered to Kṛṣṇa.
Having summoned an astrologer skilled in the scriptures and honored him / with wealth and clothes, a devoted man should first inquire about an auspicious moment.
Whatever auspicious moment he states, the commencement is praised therein; / Nabhas, Nabhasya, Īṣa, Ūrja, together with Saha and Śuci,
are the best months at the beginning of the narration; the full-moon lunar day is auspicious; / the days of the week except Tuesday and Saturday, and the fixed and gentle constellations,
under an auspicious astronomical combination and an auspicious ascendant, the commencement is always praised. / And in the daily narration of the Purāṇas, O best of sages,
a wise man should avoid the twelfth lunar day because of the defilement related to births; / but in the case of the seven-day [narration] of the glorious Bhāgavata,
there is no prohibition, O divine sage; so the knowers of old have declared. / The seven-day session of the glorious Bhāgavata is considered a great sacrifice by the wise.
Therefore, an invitation should be extended to Vaiṣṇavas on every side: / ‘An assembly of the virtuous will take place for seven days, O best of Vaiṣṇavas!
Therefore, you should come here, as Vaiṣṇavas wishing to listen.’ / And for those who have gathered, one should arrange lodging.
At a holy ford, or in a forest, or in a village, with effort / one should prepare a pavilion upon purified ground,
furnished with plantain pillars, provided with flags in the four directions. / A raised seat is also prescribed for the speaker before it, O sage.
Along the two sides, seats are prescribed for the listeners. / Facing north should be the speaker in this assembly, the best among the learned,
knowing the truth of the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures, a Vaiṣṇava, best of brāhmaṇas, / skilled in illustrative examples, steady, entirely free from desire, should be made the speaker.”
And the speaker must not be one who merely removes all doubts; / beside the speaker, another wise and learned man should be stationed to assist,
to sever the doubts of the listeners and grant the awakening of knowledge. / To eliminate obstacles to the discourse, he should first worship Gaṇeśa,
and then Durgā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the Sun, and the brahmins; / having worshipped them according to the rules with devotion, he should offer libations to the gods and the ancestors.
After that, the principal listener should worship Hari present in the book; / then, circumambulating, holding articles, cloth, and fruit
in his folded palms, O sage, he should pray to Hari residing in the book: / 'You dwell in this world as Kṛṣṇa himself in the Bhāgavata.
I have taken refuge in you, O Lord, for the sake of liberation in the ocean of worldly existence; / this desire of mine must be made completely fruitful by you,
and accomplished without obstacles; I am your servant, O Keśava.' / Having spoken thus, O sage, and having offered wealth in front of the book,
he should also pray to the speaker, bowing with folded hands: / 'O best of brahmins, form of Śuka, skilled in all the scriptures,
destroy my ignorance through the exposition of the venerable Bhāgavata.' / Having thus prayed to the speaker, he should choose five brahmins
to chant the twelve-syllable mantra, O best of sages; / and having honoured those skilled in song and instruments with gifts, garments, and the like,
he should establish them according to rule to sing praise at the end of the discourse, O sage. / But he who, casting aside anxiety for wife, wealth, home, and children,
listens with a single-pointed mind, obtains the complete fruit. / Beginning from sunrise until three and a half praharas have passed,
having recited, the meaning of the verse or of the chapter is to be explained; / at midday, O Nārada, one should rest for two ghaṭikās.
At the conclusion of the discourse, singing the praises of Keśava must be performed; / fasting should be observed by the listeners who desire its fruit.
One incapable of that should partake once of a small quantity of sacrificial food, / or only with water, or with fruit, or with milk, or with clarified butter,
he should maintain the body free of obstacles. / Hear, O Nārada, the rules for men observing the seven-day vow:
those lacking Viṣṇu's initiation are declared to have no qualification here; / chastity, sleeping on the ground, and eating from a plate of leaves,
he must observe constantly during the seven days, O best of sages. / Split pulses, honey, oil, another's food, and sugarcane juice,
what is tainted by improper disposition, what is improperly prepared, and stale food, the observer of the vow should abandon; / onions, garlic, asafoetida, radishes, and carrots,
gourds and pumpkin—a man observing the discourse vow should not eat. / Desire, anger, intoxication, greed, deceit, and envy,
delusion, malice, and violence, the vow-observer of the discourse must never indulge in.
Slander of the Vedas, Vaiṣṇavas, brahmins, gurus, cows, and vow-observers, / as well as of women, kings, and great souls, the vow-observer of the discourse should abandon.
Truthfulness, purity, compassion, silence, straightforwardness, humility, / and serenity of mind as well, the wise vow-observer of the discourse should maintain.
One desiring prosperity, one seeking a son, one desiring victory, or one whose mind is set on liberation / should listen to the Bhāgavata; one free from desires attains Lord Hari.
On the seventh day, upon its completion, one should observe a complete fast; / and worship of the speaker should be performed with gifts of cows, land, gold, and other choice articles.
One should cause a garland of sanctified tulasī to be distributed to the listeners; / and a festival should be celebrated with those skilled in singing and playing instruments.
On the following day, the wise person should also listen to the meaning of the songs; / and he should offer oblations with each verse or with the Gāyatrī according to rule:
milk-rice, honey, clarified butter, sesame seeds, grains of rice, barley, / sugar, priyāla seeds, grapes, almonds, and dates,
lotuses, camphor, sandalwood, agallochum, bdellium, / cloves, and bilva leaves, one thousand of each separately.
For the destruction of obstacles, for the removal of defects of deficiency or excess, / and for his own purification, he should recite the Thousand Names.
He should feed twelve or eighteen brahmins, or even more with faith, / with milk-rice, giving gold and a milch cow as priestly gift.
For the successful completion of the vow, here or on the full-moon day of Bhādrapada, / having fashioned a golden lion and placed upon its back
the venerable Bhāgavata after having it copied, he should present it to the speaker. / When this rite is performed, the heard Śrīmad-Bhāgavata
destroys all sins and yields excellent fruit for the listener; / it is the means to achieve dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation, and the bestower of devotion.
There is no duty in the world that is not accomplished by it; / therefore, the Bhāgavata is considered in this world superior to all Purāṇas.
The reciter is declared to be free from eighteen defects; / and the listener is regarded by the wise as free from thirty-two offences.

The Purāṇa named Śrīmad-Bhāgavata fulfills desires for human beings; / nevertheless, listening to it grants devotion only to one who is without desires.

The wishing tree called Śrīmad-Bhāgavata has the sprout of the syllable Oṃ; its birth is from good people; it has twelve cantos, radiant with devotion [...]
three hundred and thirty-two are its splendid branches; / its leaves are eighteen thousand, granting desires, easily accessible, reigning supreme above all.
Thus all has been told to you, and your desire has been accomplished: / the youthful vigor of knowledge, detachment, and devotion, which gives liberation to the world.
Sūta said: / Having spoken thus, those Kumāras, bathed in the nectar of Kṛṣṇa's feet, / devoted to the Lord and intent on uplifting the lowly, fell silent.
Hearing their words, Nārada, dear to the Lord, / spoke to them with folded hands in a voice choked with love:
Nārada said: / 'Blessed am I, graced by you who are supremely compassionate, / since Hari has been shown near at hand through the Bhāgavata week.'
While Nārada, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, was speaking thus, / Śuka, the lord of yogins, wandering about, arrived there.

Having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, lotus-eyed, the son of Vyāsa, the moon to the ocean of knowledge, / content in his own self, reciting the Bhāgavata ceaselessly in his heart at the conclusion of the recitation;
the members of the assembly, seeing him of immense splendour, immediately rose and offered an excellent seat; / and when he was seated comfortably on the seat, lotus-eyed Hari became manifest.
endowed with unexcelled virtues, became the expounder of true being.
In their midst danced the triad of knowledge and the rest, endowed with new forms. / Beholding this extraordinary celebration of praise, Hari, with a pleased mind, said:

'Choose a boon from me, O devotees of the Lord, since I am exceedingly delighted with your discourse and song of praise.' / Hearing his words, overjoyed, their hearts moist with love, they spoke to Hari:

The Kumāras said:
Through the sacrifice of seven days he is quickly propitiated, O Murāri,
for men in the most terrible Kali age, who have short lives and are distressed by hundreds of obstacles.

Such a boon we choose from you, the cause of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe, the Self of all;
there is no other desire, O Lord, for us who serve your lotus feet.

Having said, 'So be it,' Hari disappeared right there.
Very delighted in his heart, Nārada bowed down to the Kumāras.

Then Sanaka and the others, Bhṛgu and the others, and Śuka and the others,
went to their own hermitages, delighted having drunk the nectar of that story.

Bhakti, along with her two sons, was set in motion by Nārada
upon this entire circle of the earth from then on, O Śaunaka.

Śiva said:
Having heard this great narrative, Śaunaka, his heart pleased, O dear one,
questioned Sūta again, the destroyer of all doubts.

Śaunaka said:
When was it spoken by Śuka to the king? When again by Gokarna?
When by the sons of Brahmā to the divine sage? Tell this, O giver of honor!

Sūta said:
When thirty years had passed in Kali after the departure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādra, Śuka truly began the story.

When two hundred years had passed after Parīkṣit's listening,
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Śuci, Gokarṇa told the story.

Now a thousand years have elapsed in the Kali age, O twice-born one,
since the time of Parīkṣit's birth; let the sacrifice be brought to completion.

The Lord said:
Having heard his words, Śaunaka, the best of sages,
completed that sacrifice lasting a thousand years.

The Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Kūrma, Matsya, Vāmana,
Vārāha, Brahmavaivarta, Nāradīya, and Bhaviṣya,

and half of the Āgneya, they heard indeed from Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa;
these Purāṇas were indeed heard at the end of the Dvāpara age

by Śaunaka and the other excellent sages, before the beginning of the sacrifice.
When, however, Baladeva, on a pilgrimage to sacred places, arrived

at Naimiṣa, named Miśrika, being summoned by the lordly sages,
seeing Sūta seated there upon the high seat,

the blessed Rāma became agitated, like the great ocean on a full-moon day.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, on the day of breaking the fast, O Pārvatī,

in the time of the first half of the watch, because it was destined by Kṛṣṇa's māyā,
Rāma, bewildered, with kuśa grass in hand, struck down Lomaharṣaṇa.

Then all the throngs of sages broke into cries of woe;
they were exceedingly agitated at heart with grief and sorrow, O daughter of the mountain.

And devoted to forbearance, they spoke with humility to Rāma, the lord of the world.
The sages said:
O Rāma, O Rāma of mighty arms! By you, the protector of the worlds,

as if unawares, an act of violence worse than killing a brahmin was committed;
for this is the direct disciple of Vyāsa, a Purāṇic sage of great austerities.

The high seat was given to him by us in the sacrificial rite,
who set the appointed time for him to be the reciter of the eighteen Purāṇas,

and a long life in the story of the Lord of the universe, O giver of honor!
Therefore you, for the protection of the world and establishing the embankment of dharma,

have appeared, the lord of the universe, capable of punishment and favor.
Having spoken thus before Baladeva, O dear one, those sages

fell silent at once, remembering the power of destiny.
Then the blessed Rāma, the slayer of foes,

gratifying those brahmins, following the path of the world and the Veda, spoke.
Śrī Rāma said:
Listen, O brahmins, may good fortune be yours; casting away anger far off,

as I know what fulfills the desired purpose for you.
His son will become a possessor of great knowledge by my boon.

He will recite to you the entire scripture that you desire.
And let that deed be stated for which purpose I was summoned.

The Lord said:
Having heard these words of the very great-souled Rāma,
they urged the lord toward the killing of Balvala.

Then, having slain Balvala and propitiated the foremost sages,
bowing down and permitted by them, he went on his pilgrimage to sacred places.

When Rāma had gone on his pilgrimage to sacred places, the lordly sages headed by Śaunaka,
having summoned Laumaharṣaṇi and honored him, O daughter of the mountain,

installed him in that seat in order to recite the remainder,
namely, from the Āgneya onwards, ending with the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.

With delighted minds they heard seven and a half Purāṇas.
Having composed seventeen Purāṇas, the son of Satyavatī

did not attain satisfaction of mind, even through the Bhārata, O beautiful woman.
Knowing his heart to be depressed, Nārada, who sees the gods,

the blessed one, came to Vyāsa's excellent hermitage.
Seeing him, the son of Vāsavī, having honored him with a seat and the rest,

worshipped Nārada according to the prescribed rite.
Then Nārada said to him: 'Why do you, troubled in mind,

brood? Declare all that cause of your doubt!'
Thus questioned by the sage, the son of Parāśara said:

'O holy one, what is the cause of my mind's bewilderment? I truly do not know.
You, skilled in supreme knowledge, knowing that, please tell me.'

Thus informed by him, Nārada, skilled in spiritual wisdom,
spoke the supreme truth which had been spoken by Brahmā to himself.

Nārada said:
Listen from me, O son of Parāśara, to the reason why indeed your
mind appears unfulfilled, though you are the source of scriptures and a master.

Having descended into this world, the Vedas were divided by you according to sections,
and the Purāṇas were composed along with the legendary histories, O sinless one,

in which the entire duty of the three Vedas for the dwellers of the castes and stages of life
was set forth, seeing that men in the Kali age have short lives in time;

in which the eligibility of all is seen with respect to hearing and the like,
of women, śūdras, fallen brahmins, and the good; and the association with the virtuous.

Just as dharma and the other aims have constantly been described by you in them,
the greatness of Hari has not indeed been described with prominence in that manner.
In Kali, an ocean of faults, devoid of the performance of all righteous duties, O sage,

there is no resort for evil-doers without the nectar of Kṛṣṇa's story.
Indeed, this alone is the virtue in this dreadful Kali yuga for men:

that by the singing of Kṛṣṇa's praise alone they are freed from the bondage of karma.
Sacrifice, gift, austerity, ritual action, knowledge, and meditation in the Kṛta and other ages

bestow perfection; and likewise, O holy one, the singing of the divine name in Kali.
Therefore, for the deliverance of men born in Kali, you

must describe fully the Purāṇa named Śrīmad Bhāgavata,
by the promotion of which, dear friend, your mind surely
will attain satisfaction, and the worlds will achieve their fulfillment.

The Lord said:
Having thus instructed Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, that sage,
moving at will, went away singing constantly the virtues of Hari, O dear one.

And when Nārada had gone, Vyāsa, the seer of all purposes,
composed this supreme collection named the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.

Having taught the four Vedas, beginning with Paila, according to rule,
he delivered all the Purāṇa collections to Sūta.

The Purāṇa named Śrīmad Bhāgavata, equal to the Veda,
he taught to Śuka, who was detached from both the world and the Veda.

That Bhāgavata collection was heard by the son of Lomaharṣaṇa
as it was being told by Śuka to the king, the son of Uttarā.
It was truly recounted by him to Śaunaka and the other sages. / This [work] remains supreme above all the Purāṇas, O daughter of the mountain!
For men whose minds are attached to this, delight arises nowhere else, / and Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, shines within their hearts.
What you asked of me, auspicious lady, for the salvation of the world, / saying: 'Proclaim to me the glorification of the Śrī Bhāgavata,'—
all that has been expounded to you by me, O mother of Gaṇeśa, / along with various legendary histories, bestowing devotion and liberation.
Whatever person hears it with devotion, or reads this glorification, / or even approves of it, reaches the supreme state.
A twice-born man, by studying it, obtains the Vedas; a kṣatriya attains victory; / a vaiśya [attains] wealth; and a śūdra, merely by hearing it, attains liberation.

6.199.m: The sages said: / Speak in detail, O Sūta, of the glorification of the Kālindī, / to whom it was revealed and by whom, accompanied by that narrative.
Sūta said: / Once, the son of Pāṇḍu, wishing to hear auspicious knowledge from Saubhari, / approached his dwelling, bowed to him, and asked:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / O brāhmaṇa, tell me which sacred site is most auspicious among the sacred sites on the banks of the daughter of the sun, / the birthplace of Vaikuṇṭha, higher than the highest.
Saubhari said: / Once, the two best of sages, Nārada and Parvata, travelling in the sky, / looked down upon the Khāṇḍava forest, which was very charming.
Having descended from the sky there, they sat on the auspicious bank / of the Kālindī for a moment's rest, and entered the water to bathe.
King Śibi, the ruler of Uśīnara, roaming the forest on a hunt, / saw them and sat on the riverbank, waiting for their emergence.
The two sages, having bathed according to rule and donned their garments, / were saluted with bowed head by the king, and sat on the bank.
Beholding thousands of golden sacrificial posts there, / Śibi, free from pride, spoke to Nārada and Parvata.
Śibi said: / Tell me, O tigers among sages, to whom belong these sacrificial posts? / By whom was the sacrifice performed here—by a god or by a man?
Leaving aside Kāśī and the other sacred sites, what person was worshipped here through sacrifices? / What special quality is there here compared to those sacred sites, being the presence of wisdom?
Nārada said: / Formerly, Hiraṇyakaśipu, having defeated the deities headed by Śakra / and obtained dominion over the three worlds, acquired enormous pride.
Prahlāda was his son, devoted to Nārāyaṇa; / the sinful one, devoid of auspiciousness, constantly showed hostility toward him.
Because of that hostility, Viṣṇu, instantly assuming the form of Nṛsiṃha, / slew the lord of Daityas and returned the kingdom of heaven to the lord of heaven.
Having regained his own realm, the lord of gods then addressed Bṛhaspati, / bowing his head before his feet and recalling the virtues of Nārāyaṇa.
Indra said: / O guru, through the form of Nṛsiṃha, Hari, the sustainer of the world, / has given me the kingdom of the gods; I wish to worship him with sacrifices.
Tell me, O my guru, of a pure place and of brāhmaṇas; / no delay should be made here by you, my benefactor.
Bṛhaspati said: / You have the delightful Khāṇḍava forest, supremely purifying, / where bees are intoxicated by the sweet honey of ketakī, aśoka, and bakula flowers.
There flows the holy Yamunā, blessed and purifying the three worlds, / which grants heaven at remembrance, and the realm of Brahman at death.
On its bank worship Keśava, O lord of gods, with many sacrifices, / if you constantly desire the welfare of your people.
Nārada said: / Hearing the guru's words, Śakra quickly mounted his vehicle / and came to this own forest of his, which bestows auspiciousness.
Together with his guru, the gods, and the sacrificial implements, / he came here and, seeing this forest, obtained supreme joy.
Urged by his guru, Śakra, having chosen the seven sages, the sons of Brahmā, / Vasiṣṭha and other twice-borns, sacrificed to the lord of the universe.
Pleased with him, the Blessed Lord arrived along with Brahmā and Īśa / at that rite of Śatakratu, where a great celebration took place.
Seeing that triad of gods, Śakra, upright in mind, / then quickly rose from his seat and bowed together with the sages.
Having quickly descended from their vehicles, they sat after them / upon excellent golden seats, shining like fires upon altars.
Between Śambhu and Brahmā, whose bodies are white and red, Hari shone forth, / dark-hued and dressed in yellow garments, like a lightning-bearing cloud between two mountain peaks.
Śakra washed their feet and placed that water upon his head, / and filled with joy, he spoke sweet-lettered words:
Indra said: / The sacrifice performed by me today, O God, has borne fruit,
since these [deities] have been seen, who are difficult to perceive even by yogins. / By you alone, O Viṣṇu, a form consisting of the triad has been assumed.
Nevertheless, diversity caused by the qualities is false for you, like [colors seen in] a crystal. / Just as fire hidden in pieces of wood, O all-pervading one, without friction
does not manifest, so you [do not manifest] in the hearts of beings without devotion. / Devotion to you in one person may be beneficial to all beings;
The gods became happy through that [praise] made by Prahlāda: / "O God, we are worldly beings, our minds veiled by your illusion.
we do not know your essential nature truly, although serving your feet. / O Brahmā, O Mahādeva, you two also are teachers of the universe,

because of his being the teacher of all; hence you two are not distinct from him. / Whatever is spoken by speech and conceived by the mind / is his māyā alone; all that is far removed from the truth of the two [or the One].
Let a person reflect that this entire visible world of phenomena is not real; / those who worship the feet of Viṣṇu cross beyond it—whose water, O Hara, is borne upon your head.
May my deep love ever reside at the feet of the brother of Vidhi, the fear-dispeller of Kamalā, / agitated by whose glance, this whole world beginning with Mahat comes to be.

There is no other compassionate being like you, who bestow happiness even upon the side of the enemy! / If your compassion is said to be merely for dispelling the grief of your own world, O Nṛhari, that is ignorance.
Nārada said: / Having thus praised Keśava, the lord of gods, he bowed down before him / and stood attentive, desiring to hear his word, and was magnified.
Hearing the praise of that husband of Ramā thus / spoken by Indra in the assembly, the sages said: 'Excellent! Excellent!'
'O Śatamanyu, those who perform great austerities for a hundred years / do not have such devotion as yours toward Mādhava.
The eight-limbed yoga, by which renown is attained, is not easily obtained; / and renunciation of it through equanimity—devotion to him is the refuge for humans.
Whatever rite is performed according to rule with wealth earned by one's own duty, / offering it to Viṣṇu—this devotion brings auspiciousness.
He who does not censure another deity, but bows with the thought of Viṣṇu, / and does not abandon Vedic statements, is a devotee dear to this Hari.
Those who hear the virtues of Hari day after day, those who sing them, / those who remember him, those who worship the lord of the Yadus, and those who praise him—'
Those who bow down to him in servitude, those who form friendship with him, / and those who surrender their own selves to him, do not desire liberation and the like.
"O Indra, worship this teacher of the universe with devotion too; / I desire nothing from him, [and yet] I will have accomplished all my duties."

Nārada said: / When the sages had thus instructed [him], Hari, the perpetual guru, hearing his own devotion thus described—worshipful by all and bestowing the supreme station beyond the three worlds—spoke sweet words to Hari in the assembly.

6.200.m: The Blessed Lord said: / This is no wonder, O lord of the gods: the sages are exceedingly wise; / they show high honor to devotion, which is my own elevated path.
These are the teachers of wisdom to the dwellers on the surface of the three worlds, / for they continually set in motion the lost path of the Vedas.
Since you also, though attached to the pleasures of heaven, / have taken refuge in me through devotion, what is the wonder? For your preceptor is Guru [Bṛhaspati].
O tiger among gods, sacrifice to me with rites bearing copious gifts; / free from desires, you will swiftly attain my nearby abode.
At every sacrifice give numerous measures of jewels; / by name, this place of yours shall be Indraprastha.
O Brahmā, construct Prayāga here, the best of holy fords, / bringing the Sarasvatī and the Gaṅgā that purifies people.
O lord [Śiva], establish Kāśī here, and Śivakāñcī; / and Gokarṇa, and make your perpetual residence along with Gaurī.
O sons of Brahmā, skilled in wisdom and experiential knowledge, / by the power of your own yoga create seven holy fords here.
O Guru, establish the holy ford that awakens the scriptures; / even without study, let understanding of the sacred meters arise here through bathing.
And let memory of previous births arise, as well as knowledge of the Supreme Self. / I myself shall bring delightful Dvārakā here,
where the confluence of the Gomatī with the ocean took place. / And I shall make Kośalā here, and the forest of Madhu, O Vāsava,
in which I shall descend in the two forms of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. / And here [I shall place] Badaryāśrama, the seat of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
I establish it, where I dwell perpetually, O leader of the gods. / Haridvāra and Puṣkara, the two unsurpassable holy fords—
them also I establish here, solely out of desire for your welfare. / Those holy fords that are at Naimiṣa, and on Mount Kālañjara,
and those on the bank of the Sarasvatī, I shall indeed establish here. / Nārada said: Hearing this exceedingly auspicious word of Hari, and seeing it accomplished, O Śiva,
Brahmā, Śiva, and the others also did what had been spoken. / In this place comprising all holy fords, the lord of the thirty [gods],
with golden sacrificial posts, sacrificed again to the Lord of Ramā with many sacrifices; / he gave measures of jewels to the Brahmins in the presence of Kṛṣṇa:
"May Nārāyaṇa, the self of all, be pleased with this, my offering!" / From that time onward, this holy ford is called Indraprastha,
comprising all holy fords, where one who dies is not born again. / Having received those measures of jewels given by Indra, the earthly gods
bestowed on him an unfailing blessing in that assembly: / "O Indra, may Govinda be pleased with this gift of yours!
May your devotion to him also be unswerving. / O lord, formerly a hundred sacrifices were performed by you in this realm of action;
by that merit, sought with desire, the abode of the gods was obtained by you. / Now Viṣṇu has been worshipped by you through sacrifices devoid of desire.
Falling from your own station, you will become a foremost twice-born on earth; / there too, worshipping Viṣṇu by your own duty,
you will remember your own actions, the sacrifices and the like performed here. / Remembering that, abandoning your home, and wandering through holy fords,
you will arrive at this holy ford along with your father, O Śakra; / taking up the fourth stage of life, you will abandon your body here.
Then, having mounted an aerial chariot brought by attendants and radiant as the sun, / having acquired a divine body, you will attain the abode of glorious Hari."
Nārada said: / Hearing this blessing of the Brahmins, which indicated the future, / the lord of the thirty [gods] rejoiced exceedingly, O Śiva.
Having duly completed the sacrifices there, which possessed golden stakes, / he took leave of the worshipped gods headed by Mādhava.
Having honored the officiating priests, the sons of Brahmā, with wealth and other gifts, / and placing Bṛhaspati at the fore, Śakra went to heaven.
Having ruled there, endowed with devotion to Hari, O Śiva, / when his merit was exhausted, Indra descended to the earth in the city of Hāstina.
There was a certain twice-born named Śivaśarman, who had mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas; / his wife, Guṇavatī by name, was truly possessed of good qualities.
From her, at an auspicious hour, Indra, the servant of the Lord of Śrī, was born. / The astrologers were summoned, and seeing the ascendant, they spoke.
The astrologers said: / O Śivaśarman, this boy of yours will be dear to Hari; / he will uplift your lineage—we speak the truth, not falsehood.
When he is thirteen years of age, having studied the four Vedas / along with their auxiliary limbs, and being endowed with wisdom, he will indeed marry.
Having then fathered a virtuous son, he will become a forest hermit; / wandering among holy fords, the steadfast one will take up renunciation.
In Indra's Khāṇḍava forest is the Yamunā, the best of rivers; / on its bank is Hariprastha; there he will meet his death.
Nārada said: / Hearing the auspicious words uttered by the astrologers, Śivaśarman / then named his son Viṣṇuśarman.
Dismissing them with wealth, the intelligent man thought: / "Blessed am I, whose son will be a devotee of Viṣṇu!
This son of mine will fulfill all four stages of life, / and will die at an excellent holy ford; who is more fortunate than I?"
Having reflected thus in his mind, Śivaśarman had the birth rites and other ceremonies performed / for the infant on an auspicious day by the foremost twice-born.
Then, when seven years had passed, the best of the twice-born / performed the son's sacred thread investiture in the eighth year, in the month of Caitra.
Having instructed his son in the Vedas until his twelfth year, / Śivaśarman, devoted to Śiva, united him with a wife, O king.
Wise Viṣṇuśarman, having fathered a son upon his wife, / detached his mind from sensual objects toward pilgrimage to holy fords.
Approaching his father and bowing to both of his feet, / the highly wise Viṣṇuśarman, recalling the sage's words, spoke.
Viṣṇuśarman said: / Permit me, father; I shall worship this Viṣṇu, / entering the third stage of life, which brings about association with the virtuous.
Wife, house, wealth, offspring, and friends perish in a moment, / like bubbles on water; the wise person does not become attached to them.
By sacred study and by lineage, the two debts have been crossed over by me; / free from desire, I wish to sacrifice to Keśava at holy fords.
Having renounced attachment to the qualities, I wish subsequently / to stay at some foremost holy ford for as long as my prārabdha karma remains.
Spoken to thus by that son, the highly intelligent father, / remembering the words of the astrologers, said, devoid of longing for worldly life:

Śivaśarman said:
This is the time for the fourth stage of life, even for me who am free from egotism. / Abandoning worldly objects like poison, I shall partake of the nectar of Keśava.
O son, my mind no longer takes delight in the house in old age, / just as an elephant brought bound from the forest [takes no delight] in a king’s palace.
This younger brother of yours, Suśarman, will uphold the household, / which has been abandoned by us two, just as learning and good family abandon a man lacking fortune.
And your devoted mother will follow me alone as I renounce [the world], / just as radiance follows the sun at the close of day.
Therefore, unbeknownst [to others], we two, departed together with your mother, / shall go, meditating upon the lotus feet of glorious Hari.

Nārada said:
Having thus deliberated, the two seekers of liberation, in the middle of the night enveloped in darkness, / leaving behind their sleeping household, went forth from the house and departed.
Wandering together, those two, free from egotism, arrived / at this auspicious, bliss-giving holy site at Śakraprastha.
Having arrived here, calm Viṣṇuśarman, seeing the sacrificial posts / set up by himself in a previous birth, remembered his union with Hari.
And the wise one said to his father: “In the past, I was Śakra. / Sacrifices were performed here by me with the desire to please Mādhava.
Right here Keśava, affectionate to his devotees, was pleased with me, / and the Brahmins and the Seven Sages were satisfied by me with measures of jewels.
By them alone Vaiṣṇava devotion was granted, and liberation in this world. / Indeed, all holy sites were established here by Viṣṇu and the rest.
This Indraprastha was made a holy site comprising all holy sites. / Right here my death was foretold by those foremost sages.
Then the attainment of the abode of Hari—all this I remember. / These two, the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī, were brought by Brahmā from his own world,
at whose confluence this [site] is called Prayāga. / This is Kāśī, the city of Śiva, in the region east of Prayāga,
at a measure of fifty-two bows, dying in which one is not born again. / In the western part of Kāśī, at twenty-one bows,
is this Śivakāñcī, established by Śiva, which bestows immortal liberation. / This sacred field named Gokarṇa, exceedingly dear to Śambhu,
is situated in a plot of land measuring two bows. / This is holy Dvāravatī to the west of the king of holy sites,
at seventy bows, dying where one becomes four-armed. / Then to the east is Kośalā, affectionate to the people,
seen at a measure of eighteen bows, of holy sight. / This is Madhuvana, father, established by Viṣṇu himself,
in the western part of Kośalā, measuring ten bows. / Then to the north, father, is the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
and this stands in an area of land of eleven bows. / Then to the south is situated this holy site Haridvāra,
seen in an area of earth of thirty bows, difficult to attain even for the gods. / But this is the holy site named Puṣkara, the crest-jewel of holy sites,
which stands, O father, in an area of land measuring twelve bow-shots. / The distance of Prayāga and the others is a gavyūti of the great Seven Sages.
In the eastern direction there are seven tīrthas, which constitute the Tīrthasaptaka. / And in the region of the Tīrthasaptaka there are many other tīrthas,
Dying in which at every step, one is born four-armed. / At a distance of just one gavyūti west from Prayāga, on the ground,
Is the tīrtha named Nigamodbodhaka, established of old by the Guru. / There is a great distance between the Tīrthasaptaka and Nigamodbodha.
This sacred field called Indraprastha was established of old by the deities, / extending one yojana east to west, dear boy,
And four yojanas south of the Kālindī: / this boundary of Indraprastha was stated by the great ṛṣis.

And whoever abandons his body here in the presence of the triad of deities becomes unborn.
Nārada said: / Hearing these words of his son, the brāhmaṇa Śivaśarman, in auspicious intent,

Full of doubt, replied to his truthful son.
Śivaśarman said: / How should I understand this? You were once the lord of the gods;
You performed sacrifices here, and the brāhmaṇas were satisfied with jewels. / Son, act in such a way that I too may obtain the knowledge you have spoken of.
From where did you hear of this boundary of Indraprastha, / ever since which idea arose in you that you did not abandon your home?
The four Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences were studied by you from me alone. / Whence did your knowledge come concerning deeds done in a past life?
Viṣṇuśarman said: / A boon was granted to me by the ṛṣis, granting remembrance of past lives; / and only from them was this recollection of the sacred tīrtha heard by me.
Father, bathe here in the tīrtha named Nigamodbodhaka; / you will obtain hard-to-attain knowledge granting remembrance of your past life.
You will also remember the course of my previous life. / By the touch of the waters of this tīrtha, dear father, I tell you the truth.
Nārada said: / When Śivaśarman, the best of brāhmaṇas, having heard this, was about to bathe / in the tīrtha named Nigamodbodhaka for the sake of remembering his past life,
A Bhilla, pursued by a lion, came running up, / his limbs gripped with extreme terror, panting, overcome with exhaustion—
Destructive by nature, a highway robber, constantly plundering merchants, / dark-bodied, with tawny hair, short-statured, and cat-eyed,
Holding a spear in his hand, terrifying in form, like sin itself personified. / Soon afterwards, seeing the lion at a short distance, both of them,
Father and son, climbed up a nearby tree and stood there, / saying, “Alas, Kṛṣṇa, deliver [us] from untimely death!”
Seeing the lion coming swiftly to seize [him], O lord of kings, / that Kirāta, terrified, began to climb the tree.
As he was climbing, the swift lion seized him / by the feet, brought him down to the ground, and leapt upon him.
The Kirāta, even while lying beneath, indeed tore open its belly / with his spear, so that a mass of entrails gushed out drenched in a torrent of blood.
The lion, experiencing pain, then let out a dreadful roar, / crushed the Bhilla’s head, and instantly died.
When the two living beings thus met their death, O lord of the earth, / a pair of celestial aerial cars descended, along with two attendants, from the supreme abode:
Bearing the color of a fresh cloud, fashioned from crystal stone, / their ears adorned with lovely earrings, embellished with a multitude of jewels,
[An aerial car] bearing beautiful decorations with hands holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, / wearing yellow garments, adorned with golden walls,
With eyes resembling blooming lotuses, possessing ruby-studded latticed windows, / with feet having anklets producing a deep sound, tinkling with small bells,
Bearing rows of bangles on the forearms, with a lovely altar, / captivating with pearl necklaces, having chests like canopies.
With faces adorned with curling locks of hair, resplendent with high banners, / with a high archway resembling the bow of the five-arrowed god cast down by their pair of brows,
With noses putting parrots to shame, adorned with hundreds of turrets, / with the soles of their feet possessing the fine luster of fresh coral, stainless like a mirror.
The Bhilla and the lion, their divine bodies having cast off the mundane body, stood / even before the departure of their life-breaths, by the power of this tīrtha.
Having brought the two aerial cars near to them, those two attendants of Hari, / who possessed identical form, dress, and appearance, then spoke to them:
“O Kirāta, best of men! O lion, king of beasts! / Know us to have arrived from Vaikuṇṭha, two attendants of Lord Hari.

We will truly take you to that abode, where there are no sorrows. / Mounting your respective aerial cars, depart quickly without delay!”

Having mounted their respective aerial cars, that Kirāta and the king of beasts, / filled with astonishment, spoke to the two attendants of the Lord of Lakṣmī:
“O tigers among the gods, hear our words! / By the sight of you two, knowledge of the ultimate truth has arisen in us.
In this life, not even a little good deed was performed by us; / yet by your favor, remembrance of previous deeds has arisen for us.
We were meat-eaters, devoted to harming living beings, cruel in inner sense, / born in a sinful lineage, inspiring fear at mere sight.
In this world, we two were such sinners. / By what merit has this vision of you two been granted to us,

And from what merit have we achieved likeness of form [to Viṣṇu] and are going to the abode of Lord Hari?”
The two attendants said: / “Surely, because of your death in this tīrtha, fashioned of old by the preceptor of the gods,
Your sight of us has occurred, and wondrous likeness of form to us. / Attainment of the abode of the Lord of Lakṣmī shall be yours forever.
Only so long do sins, such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa, roar, / as long as sight of this tīrtha of Bṛhaspati has not taken place.
Just as darkness vanishes in this world with the rising of the sun, / so do sins disappear upon beholding the Nigamodbodhaka.
This sacred field, named Indraprastha, is indeed Indra’s purifying realm; / by him, Viṣṇu was worshipped here with sacrifices accompanied by generous gifts.
Hear the boon granted to him by Viṣṇu who was pleased: / ‘O Indra, in your sacred field, which embodies all tīrthas, those people
Who will abandon their body, even violent beings, shall indeed become equal to me.’”
Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, those two excellent attendants, taking them along, went to the abode / of Hari, having reached which one is never again submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.

6.201.m: Nārada said: / Then, descending from the tree, both father and son were greatly astonished, / having seen the attainment of the abode of Hari by even those two sinners.
Then Śivaśarman, the best of brāhmaṇas, having heard that praise of the tīrtha / uttered by the attendants, spoke to his son Viṣṇuśarman.

Śivaśarman said: / That abode which is not easily obtained by twice-born men even through austere penance practiced with ease, / was attained by a Śabara and a fanged beast! Behold the greatness of the king of tīrthas!
By the power of which even two who were sinners from birth until death / attained likeness of form to Hari, my son—what praise could suffice for this best of tīrthas?
Where is the divine form of pure sattva, hard to attain even for gods born of the lotus-born [Brahmā], / and where are the lion and the Bhilla, full of tamas? But this tīrtha works wonders!

O father, having reached the end of their deeds, a living being falls from the abode of Brahmā; / but attaining death here, fashioned by the guru of the gods, there is no falling away from the abode of Mādhava.”

Nārada said:
Having thus directly perceived the greatness of this holy site from his elder, O king, / that best of the twice-born set about to bathe there.
Having purified his mouth, teeth, feet, and mind, / tucking the five pleats of his lower garment, binding his topknot, holding darbha grass, remembering Mādhava,
touching the clay of the bank with the recitation of the verse ‘aśvakrānte’, / and making a tilaka with it, he entered the water.
Submerging himself there facing the current, he rose again; / having plunged again, remembering Hari and the Gaṅgā, the purifier of people,
and rising again, recollecting the seven sacred cities beginning with Ayodhyā, / he plunged once more into the water, his mind fixed on Govinda.
Having performed his bath according to the injunctions, he put on washed garments; / having come out, that best of the twice-born made his tilaka.
Placing darbha grass on his hands, feet, topknot, and sacred thread, self-controlled, / he duly performed the twilight ritual and likewise the threefold libation.
Having reverently offered an arghya of water accompanied by flowers to the sun, / the best of the twice-born bowed, placing his folded hands to his head.
Then that king among the twice-born performed the worship of Viṣṇu, / whose lotus feet are revered by the universe, from invocation down to food offerings.
Having completed the rites, comfortably seated, recollecting entirely / the deeds of his previous birth, he spoke to his son of such a kind.

Śivaśarman said:
“O Viṣṇuśarman, your word is not false, O father, because by bathing here / remembrance of the deeds of my former births has arisen in me.
Listen, highly fortunate one; I shall recount it before you. / Formerly I was born in a lineage of wealthy and righteous vaiśyas.
My father, named Śarabha, lived in the city of Kānyakubja, / acquiring wealth through trade, endowed with abundant righteousness and riches.
A long time passed, yet no son was born to him / whose body was seized by old age, whose mind was distressed with anxiety about that.
Day and night that foremost of vaiśyas then thought thus: / ‘Without a son, even my abundant accumulated wealth is useless.
Without a son, even a wealthy man is in debt in the world of the ancestors, / just as a cloud, though full of water, is [useless] to cātaka birds without rain.
A man conquers the universe through progeny bearing the burden of righteousness, / just as a king [conquers] an invincible enemy through the threefold power.
Pure offspring gladden the gods, ancestors, and human beings, / just as truthful and pleasant speech, when uttered, gladdens friends, adversaries, and neutrals.
Through a rising son, the father’s own spotless fame increases, / just as the water of the ocean [rises] through the moon.
Therefore one should strive for the birth of a son by means of the body or wealth; / without him, both are indeed futile for people whose lifespans are like lightning.’
As he was thinking thus, the best of sages, / Devala, who possesses knowledge beyond the senses, came to his house to bestow a boon.
Seeing him arrived, my father rose from his seat, / gave arghya and pādya, and bowed his head to the sage.
Having seated him on a seat offered with his own hand, my father / questioned the foremost sage Devala, whose sight was like that of a god:
‘Welcome, O best of sages! Is there peace in your family? / And are your austerities, study of the Veda, and observances free from impediments?
Do guests arrive at your hermitage in proper time? / Do the trees of your hermitage bear the fruit desired by your heart?
Tigers and other beasts, having come to your hermitage, / surely do not bear hostility toward deer and other animals, like brothers with brothers?
Your wandering on earth is for the joy of householders; otherwise, how / could those immersed in household cares have the vision of someone like you?
To one whose intellect rests on the dust of Hari’s feet, desire indeed exists nowhere; / nevertheless, O sage, tell me quickly the reason for your coming.’

Śivaśarman said:
Thus addressed by him, that sage Devala, worshiped by the gods, / desiring to know his inner disposition, spoke to the master of merchants.

Devala said:
‘O best of vaiśyas, abundant wealth has been amassed by you through righteousness, / by means of which, O knower of dharma, you perform daily and occasional rites.
A man obtains respect in a royal assembly by means of wealth, / just as a valiant warrior [obtains] victory in battle against enemies by means of valor.’
A householder who obtains wealth attains the highest prosperity, / just as an ox, O lord of the people, thrives on grain ripened in autumn.
Kinsmen and other people do not abandon rich men, / just as bees do not abandon a tree endowed with honeyed flowers.
Due to a lack of wealth, emaciation overtakes householders in every way, / just as in the summer season [it overtakes] the water of lakes.
That wealth exists abundantly in your house, O ruler of people. / Why then is there emaciation of your limbs? If it is not a secret, tell me now.
The vaiśya said: / "You who have ceased beneficial advice, like fathers, / what is there to be concealed from you by those like me who have attained the state of sons?"
By your favor, O best of sages, all is well with me everywhere. / Even in old age, the absence of a son is this one grief of mine.
Therefore, know this to be the cause of the emaciation of my limbs, O eminent sage. / I fear the debt to the ancestors, from which comes the downfall of men.
Devise that means, O sage, by which I may have a son. / There is nothing impossible on this earth for people like you to accomplish.
Śivaśarman said: / Having heard these words of that excellent vaiśya, Devala / steadied his mind for a moment and meditated with closed eyes.
Having perceived the cause of the obstacle to my father's offspring, / Devala, possessing suprasensory knowledge, spoke, causing him to remember:
Devala said: / Once formerly, O vaiśya, your virtuous wife / formed a wish in her mind, which I will now tell you:
‘If I become pregnant, O Gaurī, beloved of Śambhu, / then I will please you with meals accompanied by the six flavors,
with rows of incense and lamps, with betel leaves accompanied by dances, / with songs arising from the mouth of stringed instruments, and with various unguents.’
Having promised thus in the presence of her friends, your beloved / waited for that time, endowed with devotion to her.
In that very month, pregnancy occurred for your wife. / Then all her friends, with affectionate hearts, said to her:
‘The pregnancy that you desired has been granted by Gaurī. / Therefore, O fortunate lady, perform the promised worship of the goddess.
Otherwise, from an aberration, an obstacle arises if it is unfulfilled; / for in this matter, the goddesses, being pleased or angered, indeed grant boons and curses.’
Having been spoken to thus by her friends, this joyful wife of yours, / highly fortunate and devoted to her husband, said to you with modesty:
‘Lord, I wish to worship Gaurī, the granter of all desires, / by whose favor I have obtained my desired object, O master.’
O best of vaiśyas, you yourself, having heard these auspicious words of hers, / considered her, the mistress of your house, to be pregnant.
Rejoicing instantly with the highest festivity, / your honor also ordered the servants to prepare the articles of worship.
All the articles having then been brought by them, / honey, food, grapes, fragrances, and other things were given to her by you.
Then, summoning all her female companions, she said this: / 'Friends, all the materials for the worship of Ambikā have been brought.'
'Taking the articles of worship, go to Ambikā's temple / and satisfy that goddess with worship according to the prescribed rules.'
'"A pregnant woman does not go outside the house in our family"; / therefore, I will not come; you go to worship her.'
Commanded thus, those female companions took the materials and went / to the abode of Ambikā, the resort of wildly wandering bees.
crowded with mango clusters where flocks of cuckoos played in union; / adorned with clear lakes frequented by swans, sārasa cranes, and cakravāka birds;
surrounded by parrots and mainas reciting the virtues of Mahādeva; / where Umā's companion was intent on sprinkling the rows of creepers with streams of water;
whose ground was purified by the placement of the feet of Umā and Umā's lord; / with celestial trees beside water reservoirs constructed of crystal stone;
resounding with gandharvas singing to the dramatic performance of Pārvatī's lord; / where buds of mango and campaka were gently shaken by the mild breeze;
whose bowers of creepers echoed with the cries of dancing peacocks; / shining with that sporting mountain and gleaming with the brilliance of gems.
Going there, those [women] who were married bowed to the mountain's daughter; / then, having circumambulated her, they spoke to her with devotion:
'O mother of the world, reverence to you! Grant us welfare, O beloved of Śiva! / This offering has been brought for your worship; please accept it.'
'There is a vaiśya named Śarabha, and his charming wife; / she desired a pregnancy, and [vowed] worship of you upon obtaining it.'
'By your grace, O beloved of Śambhu, she conceived that child; / this offering has been sent by us for your worship.'
'In her family, a pregnant woman does not go outside the house; / therefore, she did not come, O goddess; be gracious and accept this.'
Having spoken thus to her at that time, O vaiśya, your wife's companions / duly offered that offering and worshipped with sandalwood and other substances.
Receiving no reply from Gaurī, they returned home, / and reported to their friend that the beloved of Śiva was dejected.
Hearing their words, that wife of the vaiśya, / troubled in mind, thought: 'Why was Gaurī not pleased?'
'She knows the devotion with which her worship was performed by me; / what is unknown to such beings, whether external or internal to men?'
'She knows the reason why I did not go there; / why was she not satisfied by the offering given by me?'
'I perceive no other reason for her displeasure / except that I did not go there to that delightful abode of hers.'
'What is past cannot be made otherwise today; / released from pregnancy, I will go to her temple for her worship.'
'Reverence to her, the wife of Mahādeva; may she grant welfare.' / Speaking thus, the wife of the vaiśya remained, bearing the fetus.
Śivaśarma said: / O Viṣṇuśarman, learning this past account, my father, the vaiśya, / questioned Devala, the tiger among sages, who was exceptionally knowledgeable.
The vaiśya said: / O sage, just as worship was promised by that daughter-in-law of yours, / so it was performed; tell the cause of Pārvatī's dejection.
Since she did not go there, Śivā knew that of her own accord, / and it was spoken by her companions; why did she become dejected?
Devala said: / O best of vaiśyas, listen to this reason; I tell you / why that dejection of Pārvatī arose, which destroyed the fetus.
When her companions had departed after worshipping the mother of Skanda, / Vijayā, filled with curiosity, said to Pārvatī:
Vijayā said: / O daughter of the mountain, with faith this offering was given to you by these mortal women; / why were you not pleased, O fair-faced one?
You were worshipped with incense, lamps, and food offerings for the purpose of satisfaction; / why, on the contrary, O goddess, did you fall into dejection without cause?
Devala said: / Hearing this speech of her friend, the goddess, worshipped by the foremost of the gods, / spoke to her friend Vijayā regarding the reason for her dejection toward the vaiśya [woman]:
Pārvatī said: / O friend Vijayā, I know that the vaiśya's wife, bearing a fetus, / was unable to go outside the house out of her own sense of propriety.
Her friends, sent by her, came for my worship; / but beings like me do not accept an offering made through another's hand.
If her husband had come, then it would have been auspicious; / but from her slighting me, a miscarriage will occur.
Whatever vow or worship a woman is unable to perform herself, / if she has it done by her husband, there is no violation for both of them, my friend.
Or else through a foremost brāhmaṇa, having asked her husband with single-minded devotion; / because, without coming herself, that worship of me was performed by her [companions],
and she did not have it done by her husband, therefore her pregnancy craving will be fruitless. / If both husband and wife come together with faith again
and worship me, then they will have a son. / Devala said: / That curse was not heard by you, O vaiśya, nor by your wife,
nor was it heard by her companions, nor was her favor bestowed [on them]; / because of their ignorance, O vaiśya, no son was born to you two,
not knowing the counteracting rite which grants happiness in this world and the next. / This has been told to you, O vaiśya, as the cause of your lack of offspring.
Just as Vasiṣṭha formerly told King Dilīpa, / and hearing that, the king satisfied Nandinī,
so you, O vaiśya, together with your wife, propitiate Gaurī who grants desires, / just as she, propitiated, gave a son to King Dilīpa.
Propitiate Gaurī likewise, and she will grant [a son] to you. / The vaiśya said: / Who is the king named Dilīpa, and who is that Nandinī, O sage,
by worshipping whom that best of kings obtained a son once again? / Passing over the gods headed by Maheśa, who bestow the fruits of the three classes,

why was she alone worshipped for the sake of a son by that king? / Relate all of this, O sage, which I have asked; / after hearing it, I, together with my wife, will serve the daughter of the mountain.
Śivaśarma said: / Hearing what was spoken thus with humility, O Viṣṇuśarman, by my father, the vaiśya, / that sage set out to recount the story of Dilīpa, which is exceedingly purifying in the world.

6.202.m: Devala said: / Listen, O highly wise one, to the divine and wonderful story / of King Dilīpa, which destroys the sins of those who hear it.
In the lineage of Vaivasvata Manu there was Dilīpa, the foremost of kings, / just as Prācīnabarhis was in the line of Svāyambhuva Manu.
He, the best among upholders of dharma, protecting the earth with dharma, / delighted the people with his abundant virtues as a lord of the earth.
The queen of that king was the daughter of the ruler of Magadha, / known by the name Sudakṣiṇā, like Śacī to the lord of heaven.
When a great amount of time had passed and no son was born to the queen, / that emperor, the lord of Kośala, reflected in his own mind:
'The earth-circle, held up and adorned with ocean, Mount Meru, and other precious mountains, / serves only as an ornament, not bringing offspring to me who am childless.'
'The three aims of life have been pursued in due season without contradiction, / yet in my heart, being childless, there is no happiness.'
[The king thought:] / “Viṣṇu and the foremost gods headed by Indra have been worshipped with sacrifices, / and oblong ponds, pleasure-gardens, and wells have been constructed everywhere on earth.
With cows, lands, gold, clothes, and meals endowed with the six flavors, / brāhmaṇas and guests have indeed been pleased by me with devotion.
Having uprooted rulers of the earth in battle according to dharma for sustenance, / the treasury has indeed been augmented by me with immense wealth.
Those who walk on wrong paths, the intoxicated, those who transgress their own duty, / and those who turn away from the ancestors and gods—those who deserve punishment have been punished by me.
On the five festival days, on the Vaiṣṇava day, on the day of the Sun, during rites for the ancestors, / and on the tenth and eleventh lunar days, intercourse with women was not practiced by me.
I did not neglect my own wife when she had bathed at the end of the fertile period, / and even during an infertile period, if I was requested by her at an appropriate time,
then sport was enjoyed with her, full of passion, since she was passionate. / In this way, duty, wealth, and pleasure were pursued by me according to the appropriate time.
By what fault does no offspring arise in my queen? / Vasiṣṭha is our teacher, who knows the past and the future.

He will declare that fault because of which a son is not born to me.” / Devala said: / Having reflected thus, that king, intending to go to his guru's hermitage, / entrusted the Kosala country, rich in prosperity, to his ministers.
Then, having worshipped the god who creates offspring, on an auspicious day / the couple, desiring a son, set out for their guru's hermitage.
Traversing the path in a few days, seated in a single chariot, / the couple reached their guru’s auspicious hermitage in the evening—
[to the hermitage of] the sage who had completed the Vaiśvadeva rite and was receiving newly arrived guests, / who was purifying the resident sages as well as arriving visitors
with the wreaths of smoke rising from the substances offered in the fire; / which was sluggish due to deer whose bellies were completely filled with masses of dūrvā grass,
who were approaching all around the pavilion along with herds of does; / bustling with the clamor of flocks of birds gathering in roosting trees;
where tigers, deer, and others had mutually abandoned their natural enmity; / where the sound of the Vedas had momentarily grown quiet due to the ṛṣis engaged in silent recitation and meditation;
where young boys were engaged in play that had arisen at the time of non-study. / In that [hermitage], the couple saw Vasiṣṭha, who had finished his rituals,
seated untroubled on a seat of sacred grass, attended by Arundhatī. / He bowed to the feet of his guru, and the queen bowed to his wife.
The guru also blessed him with a benediction, and Arundhatī blessed her. / Then, having honored that guest with madhuparka and other offerings,
Vasiṣṭha, the foremost among the venerable, asked him with honors: / Vasiṣṭha said: / “Hail, O best among kings! Is there prosperity in your realm,
in your family, and among your people, who follow their own duty? / Is the earth righteously protected by you, O hero?
Does your intellect, being sattvic, augment your treasury? / Do your countrymen and citizens, O king, being full of essence,
not abandon their own station, just as the oceans [do not abandon their bounds], / through affection, companionship, and cohabitation, O lord?
Are the couples in your city like Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa to you? / Do the desired vows of the subjects in your city, O best of kings, / bear their desired fruit, like the Haricandana tree in heaven?”
Devala said: / Having asked thus, that best of sages, Vasiṣṭha, the eminent ascetic, / fed the king with foods brought forth by the power of his yoga.
And Arundhatī of noble mind, endowed with great respect, / fed that queen with various condiments and cooked dishes.
The sage, having composed himself, took by the hand the king who had finished his meal, / was sitting peacefully, and was bowing down, and asked him again:

Vasiṣṭha said: / “A kingdom endowed with the seven limbs, whose subjects are devoted to their own duties, / whose kinsmen and ministers are pleased, whose warriors know the rules of weapons and missiles,
whose friends are subdued, whose enemies are removed, and whose mind is intent on the worship of Kṛṣṇa— / of what use is the kingdom of heaven to that king who possesses such a realm?
The righteous kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, having begotten sons / and having placed the kingdom upon them, repaired to austerities, O lord.
You are young and have not yet seen a son's face; you are not eligible for the performance of penance. / For what purpose have you come here, having abandoned such a kingdom?”
The king said: / “O brāhmaṇa, I have not come to your hermitage to perform penance / having abandoned such a kingdom out of a desire for heaven.
"O brāhmaṇa, what you have said is true: having placed the kingdom upon their sons, / the scions of the Ikṣvāku lineage went to the penance grove.
Even after going to heaven, this earthly kingdom was not abandoned by them; / for their lineage stands here dejected in this my form.
Just as childhood has passed, O father, and youth has arrived, / so too will it pass away today, and old age will certainly come.
After old age comes death for a man, without a doubt. / When I have met death, O brāhmaṇa, without the birth of a son,
to whom will this kingdom of the earth belong? Tell me, O guru! / Therefore, even as I dwell in the kingdom without offspring,
there is no sense of possessiveness for me here, because of its future absence. / Indeed, you thoroughly know the three aims of life, O my guru!
By what fault is no son born to me, O treasury of penance? / Seeing that fault through meditation, tell it to me quickly, O guru;

having heard it, I shall apply a remedy to obtain offspring."
Devala said:
Having thus heard the words of that lord of the earth,

Vasiṣṭha perceived the cause of the obstruction to his lineage through deep concentration and spoke.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Formerly, O tiger among kings, having served the leader of the gods,
you set out for your own palace, remembering this wife of yours who had bathed [after her period]. / As you were going in haste, O dear one, longing for offspring,
the Wish-Fulfilling Cow was standing at the root of a celestial tree on your path. / You aroused intense anger in her, whose foot-dust is worthy of worship,
as you failed to perform the customary circumambulation and obeisance. / Out of excessive fury, she cursed you: 'A son will not be born to you,
as long as you do not perform service to my offspring!' / Going in haste to provide during the fertile period, desirous of a son,
you did not hear that curse even slightly, on account of the roar of the sky's chariots. / Worship Nandinī, the daughter's daughter of that cow, [who is here] with her calf at my [hermitage],

together with this your wife; she will bestow a son upon you."
Devala said:
While the sage Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus,

Nandinī returned from the penance grove, her udders dripping milk out of affection for her calf. / Seeing her, Vasiṣṭha, best of sages, became glad of heart; / pointing out Nandinī, he spoke once more to the king.

Vasiṣṭha said:
"O king, she whose name is auspicious at the mere recollection has indeed arrived; / therefore know that the success of your objective stands close at hand.
Worshipped by you and your wife by following her in the forest and in the hermitage, / she will bestow a son upon you through her grace; of this there is no doubt.
See to it that no wild creature attacks her; / pasture her thus in the forest, O best of kings, bearing a bow against predatory beasts."

Devala said:
Saying 'So be it' to the king who spoke briefly, and to his daughter-in-law, the ascetic gave a hut for the night's sleep; / having laid down upon the earth strewn with darbha grass together with his wife, the ruler of men spent the night there with a controlled mind.

6.203.m:
Devala said:
Then, at dawn, the lord of men took the cow Nandinī, / worshipped with flowers and other offerings by the queen, and went to the forest.
Following behind the divine cow as she walked, the king went like a shadow; / following her as she ate young grass and the like, he too ate roots and wild produce;
he sat down following her when she sat in the shade of a tree; / the king also drank water following her when she drank water.
Thus the king served the Wish-Fulfilling Cow of his guru / with tender mouthfuls of grass, by warding off gadflies, and by scratching her.
Then, in the evening, she returned toward the hermitage, / purifying the body of the lord of the earth with particles of dust raised by her hooves.
Walking slowly beneath her heavy weight [of udders], Nandinī shone / as if oppressed by the great burden of the king's enterprise.
Near the sage's hermitage, the queen went out to meet her, / bringing sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, food offerings, incense, and the like;
having worshipped her according to the rule, bowing repeatedly, / and performing circumambulation, the queen stood before her with folded palms.
Having accepted that worship performed with faith by her, / resting steadily with the king, she went with the two of them to the hermitage.
While Dilīpa was thus worshipping her, firm in his vow, / twenty-one days passed.
Then, wishing to ascertain the king's disposition, / she entered a grassy cave of the Himālaya, her heart free from fear.
Then, while the king was looking at the beauty of the slopes of the Himālaya, / a lion whose approach went unnoticed seized Nandinī by force.
The cow cried out intensely with a pitiful sound like one distressed, / awakening an upsurge of compassion in the heart of that archer.
Hearing her cry of distress, that ruler of the world / turned his gaze which was fixed on the slope of the Himālaya.
Seeing that cow with tears streaming down her face, / and the lion with sharp fangs and claws upon her, the king was stricken with grief.
Perceiving that she was seized by that lion, the archer / sent forth his right arm to draw an arrow from his quiver.
Having drawn the arrow from the quiver to slay that king of beasts, / the ruler of the earth fitted it and drew it back fully with the bowstring.
His entire body rendered stiff by the lion's glance, / the king was unable to release the arrow; thereupon he was astonished.
Perceiving the king in such a state, that king of beasts / spoke in human speech, causing him to experience still greater amazement:

The lion said:
"O king, I know you to be Dilīpa, born in the solar lineage; / and know me to be Kumbhodara, an attendant of Śambhu.
This cedar tree which stands in your field of view / was nourished like a son by Pārvatī with an affectionate heart.
Once, O great king, as a wild elephant was rubbing its temples [against it], / its exceedingly soft bark was torn away.
Perceiving it in such a state, Mṛḍānī, filled with compassion, / stationed me here as a lion to protect it.
The goddess said to me: 'Listen, Kumbhodara! / Residing here, you may eat whatever creature comes here.'
From that time forth, O best of kings, obeying her command, / I reside in this cave which is guarded by all the gods.
You should not be amazed at the numbness of your own body; / great is the power of Śiva's illusion here on the Himālaya.
You cannot strike at me as if at an ordinary lion, / for the Lord steps upon my back when mounting his bull.
Turn back and protect your own body, the instrument for accomplishing all ends; / by destiny this cow has been brought here, O hero, for my food."

Devala said:
Having heard his speech addressing him as 'hero', / Dilīpa, whose body had been frozen stiff, replied to him.

The king said:
"O king of beasts, I bow to Śiva, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe, / and to Ambikā, the mother of the world.
And you are worthy of my respect, O king of beasts, as their servant; / hear the words that I speak, and instruct me: what should I do?"
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, is our preceptor known to you. / His cow named Nandinī is this one, fulfiller of all desires.
She was given by him to me to worship, for the generation of offspring. / This very [cow] has been properly worshipped by me for several days.
This mother of a young calf has been seized by you in the mountain cave. / She cannot be rescued from you by force by Śambhu's servant [like me].
How can I go before that sage without her? / She is the granddaughter of Kāmadhenu, glorious, worthy to be served by the world.
There is no other cow equal to her with which I might appease him. / Therefore, having released this cow, make me your prime food.

I offer my own body, soiled with dishonour. / Thus there would be no loss of dharma for the sage, and there will be food for you; / and for me, giving up my life for the sake of the cow, the highest state [will be attained].’
Devala said: / Having heard this, when silence was kept by the lion, O lord of men, / the king, skilled in dharma, fell down before him with downcast face.
As he was awaiting the extremely unbearable leap of the lion, / a shower of flowers dropped from above, released by the lords of the gods.
Hearing the words, ‘Arise, son!’, that king arose. / He beheld that cow like a mother, and not the lord of beasts.
Nandinī spoke this to that astonished best of kings. / Nandinī said: / ‘You were tested by me through an illusion in the form of a lion.
By the power of the sage, O king, even Antaka is unable to seize me / even in thought; whence would there be the power in other embodied beings to seize [me]?
By the offering of your own body, you were intent on protecting me. / Therefore I am pleased with you; choose a desired boon.’
The king said: / ‘The conduct that exists within embodied beings is not hidden from one like you. / Therefore, O mother, you know my desired [wish]; give that to me.
Grant me a son by the daughter of the king of Magadha, the founder of the lineage. / Nothing is impossible for pure ones like you.’
Having spoken thus, the king folded his hands and stood before him, / silent, awaiting his answer, with eyes fixed upon him.
Devala said: / Having heard these words of that king, Nandinī, / who accomplishes the purposes of the ancestors, gods, sages, and humans, said:
Nandinī said: / ‘Son, having milked my milk in a leaf-cup, drink as you desire. / When instructed by the preceptor at the hermitage, you will drink what remains again.

A son, the founder of your lineage, knower of the true nature of weapons and missiles, will be [born] to you.’ / Devala said: / Addressed thus by the daughter of Surabhi, he spoke to her with humility:
Dilīpa said: / ‘O mother, I shall drink the remainder only after every rite has been performed. / Having obtained the sweet nectar of your words, I am satisfied, O mother.
I desire nothing else, just as the cātaka bird desires water from a row of clouds. / By serving you, O mother, I have become the source of everything.
Like a fool towards knowledge that is worthy of worship by all people, / even the curse given by your grandmother became a boon to me.

Without that, whence would be the attainment of a son for me, and whence the sight of you? / Nevertheless, O mother, one like you is to be worshipped only for a boon; / for surely no one desires poison from Mahādeva, the giver of the three aims of life.’
Devala said: / Having heard those words of his, that cow, pleased, saying ‘Well done, well done!’, / addressed [him] and, of great pride, went to the hermitage together with him.
There also, worshipped by the king's wife just as on the previous day, / that cow appeared pleased, like the success of a task embodied.
Perceiving the serene face of the lord of the earth, the deer-eyed woman / knew that her desired purpose, for the sake of which the effort was made, was accomplished.
Then the couple, with the cow whose worship was duly performed, / went with her before the preceptor, having accomplished their purpose.
Looking at the two of them whose lotus-faces were cheerful, that best of sages, / a treasury of suprasensory knowledge, spoke this, gladdening [them]:
Vasiṣṭha said: / ‘O king, I know that this cow has indeed become pleased with you both; / indeed, an extraordinary radiance of face is observed in you two today.
Surabhi and the wishing tree are renowned as fulfillers of desires. / Having worshipped her offspring, if one's purpose is accomplished, what wonder is there?
She gives every wish when praised even from afar, O sinless one; / what then when served with faith nearby, like the celestial river?
Through knowledge, the wonderful test made by her of you was known to me; / O lord of the earth, you also protected your own dharma, and just as that [happened].
In you, she recognized the favour of my mind as the disposition in herself, / and was pleased just as Kamalā is with Hari, or as Pārvatī attaches herself to Giriśa.
Let this night be spent here together with your wife, intent upon the worship of the cow. / O noble king, you will go to your own city tomorrow, the rite being completed.’

Devala said: / ‘O vaiśya, having thus worshipped the cow, having obtained his desire along with his wife, / in the morning, having yoked his chariot and having received the instruction of the preceptor, he went home.
Within a few days, Raghu was born to that Dilīpa, / by whose name the lineage of Raghu became renowned on earth.
The man who recites this story of King Dilīpa / shall obtain wealth, grain, and a son in this world, O vaiśya.

O Śarabha, for the sake of obtaining an excellent son, quickly please Gaurī together with her according to your intellect; / she will indeed give you an irreproachable son, possessed of virtues, the bearer of the family’s burden.’

Śivaśarma said: / Having related this holy and most charming conduct of King Dilīpa to Śarabha, / and having instructed him in the rite for the worship of Ambikā, the sage went to his desired destination.

6.204.m: Śivaśarma said: / ‘O Viṣṇuśarma, then the vaiśya Śarabha together with his wife, / having taken the worship materials, went to the temple of glorious Caṇḍikā.
There, having bathed according to rule, filled with devotion, / they worshipped Caṇḍikā with flowers, incense, and lamps, wishing for a son.
Worshipped by the two of them with faith for seven days, Ambikā, / having become visible with a serene mind, spoke with [her] voice.
Pārvatī said: / ‘O vaiśya, I am pleased with your very firm devotion; / I grant you a son, O virtuous one, for whose sake you strive.
Go, do not delay, to the Indra-forest and Khāṇḍava; / there is an excellent, greatly holy sacred site named Indraprastha.
There is a sacred site there, awakening the Vedas, granting all desires, / created by Bṛhaspati; having bathed there, desiring a son,
by your bathing there, O dear one, a son will surely be born to you. / Having bathed there, O dear, even I obtained Skanda, the slayer of the enemies of the gods.’
Śivaśarma said: / Having heard these words of the goddess, my father along with his wife / came here to this good sacred site and bathed, desiring a son.
He gave a hundred cows with accessories to the brāhmaṇas, / and the wise man duly gratified the gods and the ancestors here.
Having dwelt there for seven nights with restrained minds, / the couple went to their own home, their lotus-faces blooming with the attainment of their desired object.
In that very month the embryo developed day by day in my mother; / after the ninth month had passed, I was born in the auspicious tenth.
O Viṣṇuśarman, what has been told to you by me is an ancient event; / all this was heard from my father's mouth when I was just twenty years old.
Once, seeing me capable of managing household affairs, my father, / attaining detachment from the world, handed over the household to me.
And that righteous soul, his mind attached to Govinda, spoke to me, / censuring attachment to sense-objects and praising devotion to Viṣṇu again and again.
The father said: / "O wise one, old age has arrived, and my hair has turned gray. / I shall serve the lotus feet of Govinda, served by the virtuous.
By serving Him, the mind becomes pure and very steady; / that man, content in the self, desires nothing at all.
Free of desire, experiencing natural good and bad deeds through pleasure and pain, / when they are exhausted, casting off the body, he becomes unborn.
Material wealth and the pleasure of the guṇas last only so long as the bliss of consciousness is not attained; / upon attaining that, they become worthless, like buttermilk compared to nectar.
Hari's māyā is powerful, which deludes the embodied soul; / he does not know what is beneficial for him, just like intoxication from liquor.
Through knowledge and ignorance, He brings about active life and cessation at will in due time, / for that Lord engages in child's play.
When action prescribed by the Veda is performed by one desiring its fruit, / that is worldly action, dear one; superior is the offering of those actions to the Lord.
Just as burnt seeds do not sprout despite effort, / so actions offered to the Lord of the Universe without desire [bear no binding fruit].
The dissolution of actions that bestow pleasure and pain is liberation, / whereas their generation is bondage—this is the conclusion of the scriptures.
Therefore, performing the action taught by the Veda without desiring any fruit, / I shall wander among holy bathing places, holding devotion to Hari in my heart.
Thus experiencing commenced actions without dreading others, / I shall destroy the disease of worldly existence by drinking the medicine of company with the virtuous."
Śivaśarman said: / "Having heard such words of that father of mine, / I said—O Viṣṇuśarman, listen to it in truth:
The vaiśya's son said: / 'These people are hard to please; they will tell of no glory of yours, [saying]: / "He has gone away, fleeing in distress from a wicked family."
This is the Viṣṇupadī, father, the purifier of the three worlds; / remembered even from afar, she takes away sin. Why do you abandon her?
A sinful person, father, who dies even in Magadha, / his sins cast off in the Gaṅgā, goes to heaven. Cast aside what is inauspicious.
