The sixty thousand sons of the great-souled Sagara, / burned by Kapila's wrath, went to heaven by her touch.
Leaving her, this staircase to heaven that even grants liberation, / attended by seekers of liberation, father, do not go elsewhere.
Do not despise the nearby Gaṅgā, honored by the gods; / served, she will grant whatever you desire, fortunate one.'"

“Even animals, when their life ends in its water without knowledge,
reach Brahman. How then can you abandon it?”

Śivaśarman said:
Hearing this speech, my father, lover of truth,
lived in his house, turned away from all sensual pleasures.

Taking a bath every day in the Gaṅgā at the three divisions of the day,
he regularly went wherever a Purāṇa was [recited] in a house.

Once, the wise man, listening to the greatness of the Yamunā’s holy sites,
heard there, O son, the glorification of this holy site:

“Compared to Avimukta, Haridvāra, Prayāga, and Puṣkara,
Ayodhyā, Dvārikā, Kāñcī, Mathurā, and other places,

the merit of this [place], containing all holy sites, is a hundred times greater.”
Having heard this spoken by that learned Sūta, my father,

abandoning his home, went to that holy site unnoticed by everyone,
just like us two, noble one, serving the feet of Govinda.

Having come here, noble one, desiring liberation, my father,
bathing at the three divisions of the day at the holy site Nigamodbodhaka,
lived for several months indeed at this best of holy sites.

Performing his daily rites, the wise man, free from desires even in the house of Brahmā,
was suddenly struck once by an extremely severe fever.

Through his great torment, he lost consciousness and swooned;
for a muhūrta my father remained in that condition, fainting.

Afterwards, his life-breath returning, reflecting on this at that time:
“Alas, what distress has befallen me! My righteous son is far away,

the wise one who would comfort me whose limbs are tormented by fever!
The terrible sin of approaching an illicit woman that was committed by me,

for that not even an expiation was performed; what will be my fate?
My son will come; to him I shall give my wealth.”

“What was hidden by me in the house was not seen by me either.”
Śivaśarman said: As he was thinking thus, a traveler oppressed by rain,

suffering from the cold, his body trembling, entered the hut then.
Seeing him lying down, going once again near him,

recognizing, “This is an ascetic,” the wayfarer bowed with his head,
and said: “Why are you asleep, O sage? The twilight has arrived.

The sun is setting; this is not the time for your sleep.”
Upon these words being merely spoken by the traveler, my father,

Śarabha, his limbs burning with fever, said to him somehow: “Ah!
Śarabha said: Let the word that I speak before you be heard, O traveler!

Hearing it, O good man, who have arrived by my good fortune, please do this:
I am a vaiśya named Śarabha; my home is in Kānyakubja.

Though forbidden by wife, friends, and sons, I came here,
having heard the glorification of this holy site proclaimed from the mouth of my son.

A few months have passed, O good man, since I arrived;
three days have now elapsed while I have been suffering from fever.

My vital breaths had departed, and today have returned again;
surely some remainder of life still remains for me, O good man,

since, having seen the abode of Yama, I have returned once more!
By some rise of fortune you have arrived here near me.

Lead me to my home, friend; I shall give you much wealth!
I will give even more upon reaching home; show mercy, O ocean of compassion!

Digging in the ground here, take my wealth.”
Śivaśarman said: Hearing this, that evil-minded rustic, addicted to sensual pleasures,

greedy for wealth, said to him: “I will carry out what you said.”
Having said this, digging up the wealth from that spot of ground then,

he placed it before Śarabha, and the traveler said:
The traveler said: “This wealth has been extracted by me from your ground, O lord of vaiśyas.

Give it quickly to me to bring a litter,
mounting you on which, suffering from fever, I may take you to your dwelling.”

Śivaśarman said: Addressed thus by him, he then gave three palas of gold.
He too, taking the father's wealth, went to Lavaṇapattana.

Having stayed for one night, he brought a litter with its accoutrements,
along with bearers, O son, having given two palas of gold.

The two palas [remaining] were taken by that very one of unrighteous mind.
Having mounted Śarabha, the best of vaiśyas, onto the litter,

that traveler set out, urging the bearers toward Kānyakubja.
Taking the water in a water-pot from this excellent holy site,

giving it little by little to drink to him who was tormented by thirst, the traveler went on.
Then they alighted on the bank of a lake along the way to eat.

Having bathed and eaten, they set out again from that place with haste.
Traversing some distance, suffering from thirst, from the water-pot

having drunk water, he also gave [it] to drink to that Śarabha who was tormented by thirst.
Then a certain terrifying rākṣasa, named Vikaṭa,

wandering in the lonely forest, caught sight of them as they went.
Seeing them, seized by hunger, swift, with mouth wide open,

he rushed toward them, making the earth tremble with the striking of his feet.
Arriving swiftly at their side, those bearers and that traveler

he seized along with the palanquin, and, moving in the air, whirled them around;
by that very whirling, when their lives were gone, he dashed them to the earth.

He ate their flesh, and drank their blood from the palanquin.
“Where will this man stricken with disease go before me?

Him I will eat, but first I shall drink water.”
Resolving thus, the water from the water-pot of this holy site

that foremost of night-roamers threw into his mouth at that time.
As soon as the water was thrown in, memory of his previous birth

arose, and he turned back from the slaughter of that Śarabha.
The sin committed in his previous birth also came to his memory,

by which he had become a rākṣasa despite being born a brāhmaṇa.
Remembering his sin, quickly approaching near Śarabha,
the rākṣasa, having attained knowledge, spoke to my father:

The rākṣasa said:
“O tiger among men! Who are you, and who are these people
who were eaten by me, a vile rākṣasa of terrible form?

Of which excellent holy site is this water, by whose power
even for me, a sinner, memory of my previous birth has arisen?”

The vaiśya said:
“I am a vaiśya, O best of rākṣasas; my home is in Kānyakubja.
Wandering among holy sites, I arrived at Indraprastha.

He was requested by me: ‘Bringing a litter, take me home.’
And that traveler, bringing a litter quickly,

and mounting me on it, the firm man set out toward my home.
That traveler and those bearers of the litter have now been eaten

by you. And of which holy site this water is, hear that:
In the Khāṇḍava forest of Indra there is the Yamunā, best of rivers.

On its bank is Hariprastha, a holy site best among the best holy sites.
There is the holy site of the teacher of the gods, accomplishing all aims,

Nigamodbodhaka, by drinking whose water your memory was born.
All this has been recounted to you, since I was questioned here by you.

I ask you something, O night-roamer; tell it quickly!
Do you remember here now the action done in your previous birth?
Say, what sin was committed by you, because of which you became a rākṣasa?”
The rākṣasa said: / "Formerly I was a brāhmaṇa in an auspicious family of Vedic scholars, / but of evil conduct and unrighteous mind. Listen, I tell you all.
Indeed, continually gambling with dice alongside experts in it, / I lost vast wealth, my own and my father's.
My father reported my deeds to the king, and by his men / I was expelled penniless from the city. I went to a nearby village.
There was a friend of mine, an excellent brāhmaṇa named Devaka; / by him I was sheltered in his house, showing me hospitality for a long time.
Living there comfortably, overcome by lust, I forcibly enjoyed / his beautiful wife once when my friend had gone away.
Having consumed deadly poison, that virtuous woman died instantly; / seeing her, I fled in the dead of night, enveloped in darkness.
Fleeing swiftly, I was seized by the king's servants; / [shouting], 'This is a thief!' they severed my head with a sword.
Entering me, who was dead, into a body of torment, Yama's servants / threw me into the dreadful Raurava hell at Yama's command.
Having suffered intense torment there for sixty thousand years, / by that very sin I became a rākṣasa.
A hundred years have passed in the state of a rākṣasa, O lord of the people; / tell me the means by which I may attain release from this.
I tell you of the merit that was performed, good sir, listen respectfully, / by which this water of the excellent holy place entered my mouth.
In that very birth, having observed the fast on Hari's day, / out of association rather than desire, O vaiśya, I kept awake at night.
Then, on the twelfth day, having bathed and preparing to eat, / a certain Vaiṣṇava, bearing the form of Viṣṇu, arrived at my house.
Angered upon seeing him, I spoke harsh words before him: / 'Where are you going, you hypocritical wrongdoer, among the women?'
When he was spoken to thus by me, the steadfast [sage], equal in honour and dishonour, / silently walked out of my house and departed,
Then my devoted wife, coming toward him, / fell at his feet and brought that holy man back to the house.
Though insulted by me, the great-souled man felt no anger, / nor did he feel joy when honored by her, for he looked upon enemy and friend alike.
Having worshiped him properly and seated him on a seat, she said, / 'Feed him food, lord of my life; may the three worlds conquer!'
thus addressed by that virtuous woman, I, dejected of face, said to that noble-minded [guest] with a bright countenance: / “Rise, appease your hunger.”
Having said this, that slender-waisted woman, urged [by me], / washed his feet and seated him again upon an excellent seat.
I gave a vessel filled with food to that discerning man / and water in his hand, repeatedly impelled by that virtuous woman.
Having eaten at his leisure, undisturbed, that righteous soul / went away, chanting: 'Hare Rāma, Hare Kṛṣṇa!'
This merit was performed in my former birth, O vaiśya, when urged by my wife, / by which this water of the holy place was brought to me."
Śivaśarman said: / "O Viṣṇuśarman, while the rākṣasa stood there after speaking these words, / that traveler and those who had carried him, possessing divine bodies, spoke from the sky.
The palanquin-bearers of the traveler said: / 'O virtuous lord of the people, though we met an untimely death, / by your grace, having drunk this water, we have attained godhood.
Since we set out in your company, O lord of the vaiśyas, out of greed for wealth, / our desire for wealth was entirely gone at the time of death.
Indeed, as the water of this king of holy places remained in our bellies / at the moment of death, by its power friendship with the Lord of Wealth was attained.
We bow to you; we are going to the city of the Lord of Wealth, O master, / by celestial chariots brought by his attendants and adorned with various gems.
Depart, do not delay, to the holy place that teaches the Veda; / along with this one, O good man, quickly liberate him as well!'"
Śivaśarman said: / "Having spoken thus, dear one, they departed in the northern direction completely, / making heaven and earth resound with the chiming of bells from their celestial chariots.
Then the vaiśya, my father, spoke to that night-wanderer. / Śarabha said: / 'Rise, take me quickly to the holy place that teaches the Veda.
Afflicted with fever, I cannot go there on foot; / there is no one other than you who can take me to that holy site.
Śivaśarman said: / "Saying, 'So be it,' and comforting the vaiśya, that night-wanderer / placed him on his shoulder and went swiftly to that purifying holy place."
Both of them, the merchant and the rākṣasa, dwelt there, / performing merely ablutions in that highest of all holy places.
Then, having heard of the great and severe pain of my father, / I was urged on by my mother and set out from my home.
Arriving here, I saw him afflicted with a severe fever. / I bowed my head to him, and he blessed me and spoke:
Śarabha said: / For what purpose have you come here on this long road, my son? / Stay for a few days, performing your duties here.
A friend of mine, a rākṣasa named Vikaṭa, is approaching. / Rise up and prostrate with your body like a staff at his feet.
You must not fear him, for he has abandoned violent acts and the like; / having now reached the sacred ford, he stays near me.
Śivaśarman said: / Thus addressed at that time by my noble father Śarabha, / I rose and fell prostrate like a staff at his feet upon the earth.
Lifting me up with both arms, the rākṣasa embraced me tightly, / and said, 'Welcome, son of my friend,' bestowing a blessing.
The rākṣasa said: / Fortunate are you, my son, that you have come here / upon hearing of the terrible fever-affliction of your righteous father.
You pay your debt to your father by offering water with sesamum in the sacred ford. / Having bathed, perform your rites; you will remember your past birth.
Śivaśarman said: / Thus addressed then by him, I entered into the sacred ford's excellent waters to bathe, / remembering, my son, the good and evil of my previous birth.
Having bathed according to rule, I returned right here to my father's side, / and asked about the story of the rākṣasa: 'From where has this righteous mind of his arisen?'
The account of the rākṣasa, the beasts of burden, and the traveler was recounted by my father. / Having heard it, I indeed praised this king of holy fords.
'When my father becomes free from disease, then / I will go home'—so resolving, I stayed here for ten days.
Within ten days, my son, the death of my father / occurred, half-submerged in the water, as the king of holy fords looked on.
Then, mounted upon Garuḍa and bearing Śrī upon his chest, / Viṣṇu himself arrived, his body like a fresh cloud,
clad in yellow garments, four-armed, with eyes reddish like lotuses, / accompanied by Brahmā, Indra, and the celestial beings, along with the foe of Andhaka,
being attended by Kinnaras singing the multitude of his virtues, / and being praised on all sides by Hāhā, Hūhū, and others.
Having granted his own form and placing him on Garuḍa, / he ascended to Vaikuṇṭha with my father, surrounded by Brahmā and the others.
Beholding my father attain the form of Viṣṇu, I thought, / observing this in my heart, then the dawn of ultimate reality arose:
'The majesty of this crest-jewel of holy fords cannot truly be described, / in half of whose water a dying creature becomes four-armed!
I must by no means abandon this king of holy fords / of manifestly firm greatness, out of thirst for wealth, relief from illness, and the like.
I must remain here in my father's hut / as long as the fruits of commenced actions are experienced on the face of the earth.'
Reflecting thus and having performed the funeral rites for my father, / I stayed, longing for liberation, in the company of that rākṣasa.

6.205.m: Śivaśarman said: / Once, seeing a milk-giving cow sunk in the mire at this great holy ford, / that foremost of rākṣasas entered it to rescue her.
'In protecting a cow lies great dharma; heavenly destination comes to the protector'— / while reflecting thus in the midst, he was seized by an alligator.
Dragged down beneath the waters, his belly filled with water, / his body crushed by it, he instantly gave up his life.
Assuming a divine form, an aerial chariot brought for him / by an attendant sent by the gods headed by Indra,
as he was departing, that foremost of night-wanderers was questioned by me: / 'Having met death here at this great, rarely attained holy ford that bestows liberation,
how has the attainment of the realm of the gods come to you, O noble-minded one?' / Thus addressed, he said to me: 'Such was my wish here, O sinless one.'
When that virtuous soul had gone to heaven, the realm of the meritorious, / alone then, I took Viṣṇu as my true refuge.
Walking, standing, sleeping, waking, and bathing constantly, / I meditated with single-minded focus on that very Lotus-Eyed One:
'O Hari, I have taken refuge in your lotus feet; / my mind has no desire for the status of Brahmā, Maheśa, or Indra!'
Praying thus, my son, to that very Supreme Being, / I dwelt at this great holy ford, making my mind detached from sense objects.
Viṣṇuśarman said: / If your death occurred while dwelling at this great holy ford, / how is it that you have attained rebirth again? This is my doubt.
Even those who, abandoning the sacred boundary of this holy ford out of greed for wealth, / were killed by the rākṣasa—the traveler and the beasts of burden—
went to heaven simply by drinking the water of this best of holy fords. / Likewise, even that rākṣasa, meeting an untimely death in this place,
went to heaven by his own desire before your very eyes, killed by a crocodile. / Surely your death did not take place there, since rebirth is seen.
Nārada said: / Hearing the auspicious words of his son through Śiva, Śivaśarman / told the former account, the reason for his own birth.
Śivaśarman said: / Viṣṇuśarman, listen to this reason for my birth; / I shall relate it before you; having heard it, be free from doubt.
Once, while I was established in meditation during the worship of Viṣṇu, / Durvāsas, angry by nature, arrived at my hermitage.
Not knowing that he had arrived, devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, / I remained in that state for a long time, recollecting his name.
Having stood before me for an hour, fainting with rage, / that sage, his eyes deeply reddened, said this loudly to himself:
Durvāsas said: / 'Ah, I am the son of Atri, born of the womb of Anasūyā, / a portion of Śiva, yet I am utterly disregarded by this mortal!
By me Śakra was cast down from kingship over the three worlds; / even me this evil-minded mortal disregards!
Who is there that does not fear me as if from the fire of cosmic dissolution? / Leaving aside the triad of gods, the worlds are under my control!
Which deity is this fool meditating on, absorbed in contemplation? / Why does it not awaken him, seeing that Yama stands before him in bodily form?
Surely he meditates upon the god Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world, / satisfied by the nectar of whose meditation he has no external awareness.
Whether he meditates on Hari, or Brahmā, or Śaṃbhu, or another, / he must by all means be punished by me, for he has insulted me.'
Śivaśarman said: / Having reflected thus, he awakened me, despite my good intention, / and as I awoke, he cursed me, his eyes red with anger:
'Since in your heart, having disregarded me, a desire was formed during your meditation, / it shall not be fulfilled for you in this birth, but in every way it will happen [in the next]!'
When, having spoken thus, O dear one, that sage born of Atri departed, / then he was seized by the feet by me, who was terrified with fear.
And he was addressed: “O best of sages, let it be forgiven, let anger be cast away! / Those like me do not truly comprehend the actions of those like you.”
"You have pronounced a dreadful curse, which is now considered [unavoidable] by me. / Be gracious to me, bowing low, and grant me a favor at the curse's end!"
Addressed thus, Durvāsas abandoned his rage and became calm. / How could this not be proper, O dear one, since he is Śiva himself?
Becoming still, that wise best of brahmins said to me: / "Attaining death right here, you will not obtain birth again."
Thus having shown grace to me, the sky-clad sage departed, / having stayed for that day, O dear one, honoured with hospitality by me.
"The sage's word is not false," thinking thus also,
he went to his own home, carrying regret in his heart, [thinking] thus: / "Alas! For me, who constantly meditate and dwell in holy pilgrimage sites and hermitages,
the vision of the lord of Śrī has become hard to obtain in this birth, / as for a cātaka bird [the sight] of a cloud during the burning heat of summer.
From where did this obstructor of my journey to Vaikuṇṭha come to me, / like an unseasonal raincloud releasing water for a person about to set out?
There is surely no fault in the sage; it is truly the will of Hari himself. / For having granted a good vision, another birth has been ordained for me.
By me, terrified of saṃsāra, Hari's lotus feet must be clasped, / like a tree by a traveler scorched by the summer sun.
What is the use of wealth, children, wives, and other impermanent relatives / to me who repeatedly utter, 'Govinda, Supreme Bliss, Rāma'?
Sitting like an indifferent person among family members, worshipping Hari, / I will experience only what is begun by past deeds (prārabdha), holding off other actions."
Thinking thus, dear one, after a few days / I reached my own home, having bathed in the water of Hari's feet [the Gaṅgā].
The death of my father was told to my mother and to my kinsmen; / having heard it, they also grieved, but did not shake my steady [resolve].
Without desire for the worlds such as the world of Satya, living at home, / I met death on the bank of the Gaṅgā frequented by sages.
By the curse of the sage Durvāsas, I was born in a Vaiṣṇava family, / and obtaining death here at this true holy place, I will attain the abode of Hari.

Nārada said: / Thus, O fortunate one, those two best of twice-born ones, staying at that holy place established by the teacher of the gods [Bṛhaspati], / having narrated their past deeds to each other, remained contemplating the sprout-like feet of Hari.

Contemplating Hari, the lotus-eyed, four-armed one whose form is dark as a raincloud, / shining with the ornaments of his own weapons, they attained resemblance of form (sārūpya) with Hari right there by remembering [him].
This holy sacred field is named Indraprastha; / its legend has been told; hear its fruit, O Śiva:
Whatever merit arises from bathing in the Gaṅgā and whatever arises from the gift of a maiden, / a man attains that merit with faith from listening to this.
Whatever fruit arises on earth from the gift of a cow when a son is born, / and from bathing in the water of the Godāvarī when Jupiter is in Leo,

that fruit arises from listening to this; there is no doubt here. / Therefore, there is no other holy place yielding all desires than this best of holy places, / where upon dying, even animals surely become four-armed.
